title: Contract Administration: CORs, Modifications and the Changes Clause
summary: After award the contracting officer is the only person who can change the contract, and everything else in administration flows from protecting that line. The COR is the KO's designated eyes and ears for technical surveillance with no authority to direct changes, commit funds, or alter the terms. Modifications are either bilateral, signed by both parties, or unilateral under a clause that authorizes the KO to act alone - and the Changes clause is the one that requires the contractor to keep working while the money is sorted out.

sections.heading: COR designation and limits
sections.body:
A COR is designated in writing by the contracting officer to perform technical monitoring and surveillance - the KO's eyes and ears, not a second contracting officer. Under DFARS 201.404-70 and its PGI a COR must be designated for service contracts, and in practice for any contract where surveillance is needed, nominated by the requiring activity as early as practicable in the acquisition process.

The designation letter is the whole game. It states:

- The specific authorities delegated and the limits - inspect and accept for the Government where delegated, monitor performance, review invoices for technical sufficiency, maintain a COR file.
- What the COR may never do: change the price, quantity, quality, delivery schedule, period of performance or any other term; authorize work outside the scope; direct the contractor's employees; obligate funds; or make any commitment affecting cost.
- The training and certification the COR must hold, the appointment effective date, and the requirement to report to the KO.

A COR who directs a change creates an unauthorized commitment, ratifiable only under RFO FAR 1.405 if at all. Say the sentence on the board: the COR has no authority to change the contract.

sections.heading: Post-award orientation
sections.body:
The post-award orientation conference - the start-of-work meeting - exists to make sure the contractor and the Government have the same understanding of the contract before anyone spends money. RFO FAR 42.302(a)(3) lists conducting post-award orientation conferences among the contract administration functions.

What to cover: the scope and the deliverables; the QASP and how surveillance will run; invoicing and payment procedures including who certifies receipt; security, access and installation requirements - which overseas means SOFA status, base access and any invited contractor processing; government-furnished property and information; the key personnel and the points of contact on both sides; the COR's authority and its limits, said out loud in front of the contractor; how changes are requested and who may authorize them; and reporting requirements.

What is inappropriate: renegotiating price or terms; directing work beyond the contract; letting the customer give the contractor a to-do list; anything that creates an expectation of extra work. The orientation clarifies the contract; it does not amend it. If something surfaces that genuinely needs to change, that is a modification action afterward, signed by the KO.

sections.heading: Modifications: bilateral, unilateral and administrative
sections.body:
A contract modification is any written change in the terms of the contract, and RFO FAR Part 43 governs.

- Bilateral modification, a supplemental agreement, is signed by both the contractor and the contracting officer. Use it to definitize a change order, to reflect a negotiated equitable adjustment, to incorporate a settlement, or to make any change that requires the contractor's consent. It is the preferred vehicle because it closes out the price and the schedule at the same time as the change.
- Unilateral modification is signed only by the contracting officer. Use it to make administrative changes, to issue change orders under the Changes clause, to issue termination notices, and to exercise options under an option clause. The authority must come from a clause already in the contract.
- Administrative change is a unilateral modification that does not affect the substantive rights of the parties - a change in the paying office, an appropriation data correction, an address change.

On the board, when handed a scenario, say which type and which clause gives you the authority. A modification with no clause authority and no contractor signature is not a modification - it is a problem.

sections.heading: Scope: the question before every modification
sections.body:
Before you touch a modification, ask whether the change is within the scope of the contract. If it is outside the scope, it is a new procurement requiring its own competition or a justified sole-source authority under Part 6 - you cannot buy new work under an old contract.

The test courts and GAO apply: would the modified work be materially different from the work competed? Look at whether the solicitation put offerors on notice that this kind of change could occur, the magnitude relative to the original effort, whether the nature or type of work changes, and whether other firms would have competed differently.

- Within scope: a quantity change inside the stated variation, a design refinement under the Changes clause, a period adjustment consistent with the terms.
- Outside scope: adding a new line of work, a major increase in quantity beyond what was competed, a change of the end item.

A cardinal change - so far outside scope it is effectively a new contract - is both protest exposure and potential breach. Document the scope analysis and bring in counsel before signing.

sections.heading: The Changes clause and the duty to proceed
sections.body:
The Changes clauses at RFO FAR 52.243-1 through 52.243-7 give the contracting officer the unilateral right to make changes within the general scope of the contract - in the drawings, designs or specifications; in the method of shipment or packing; in the place of delivery; and for services, in the description of services or the place of performance.

The rules a board wants:

- Only the contracting officer may issue a change order. Anyone else's direction is a constructive change at best and an unauthorized commitment at worst.
- If the change causes an increase or decrease in cost or in the time required for performance, the KO must make an equitable adjustment and modify the contract.
- The contractor must assert its right to an adjustment within the period stated in the clause, normally 30 days from receipt of the change order, though the KO may consider a late assertion at any time before final payment.
- RFO FAR 43.301(b) and the clause require the contractor to continue performance as changed while the adjustment is negotiated. Disagreement over money is not a stop-work authority, and stop-work is a separate clause.

sections.heading: Requests for equitable adjustment and claims
sections.body:
A request for equitable adjustment is the contractor asking for more money or time under a clause of the contract - Changes, Government Delay of Work, Differing Site Conditions, Suspension of Work, Government Property. It is not automatically a claim.

My process:

- Acknowledge receipt and get the REA in writing with the specific clause relied on, the factual basis, and a cost breakdown by element.
- Determine entitlement first, then quantum. Is there a compensable change, did the Government cause it, and does a clause give relief? If entitlement fails, no amount of cost detail matters.
- For DoD, the REA certification at DFARS 252.243-7002 applies above the stated threshold - the contractor certifies the request is made in good faith and the supporting data are accurate and complete.
- Analyze cost with proposal rigor - cost analysis, audit support if the dollars warrant, and the Part 31 cost principles.
- Negotiate and definitize by bilateral modification with a release of claims.
- If it arrives as a certified claim over $100,000 under the Contract Disputes Act, the clock runs and appeal rights attach.

Contract Administration and Audit Services - part page.
Conduct post-award orientation conferences - contract administration function.
Contract Modifications - part page.
Change orders - the contractor must continue performance as changed (legacy FAR 43.201(b)).
Changes - Fixed-Price; the Changes clause family runs 52.243-1 through 52.243-7.
Ratification of unauthorized commitments (legacy FAR 1.602-3).
Requests for equitable adjustment - contractor certification.
Contract Disputes Act claim certification for claims exceeding $100,000 (legacy FAR 33.207).

board_angles.q: What is the role of your COR and what can they not do?
board_angles.a: The COR is my designated technical eyes and ears - surveillance under the QASP, invoice review for technical sufficiency, documentation and reporting - and they may never change price, quantity, quality, schedule or any term, direct contractor employees, obligate funds, or authorize work outside the scope.

board_angles.q: When would you use a bilateral versus a unilateral modification?
board_angles.a: Bilateral when the change needs the contractor's consent - definitizing a change order, a negotiated equitable adjustment, a settlement; unilateral when a clause already in the contract gives me the authority to act alone - administrative changes, change orders under the Changes clause, option exercises and termination notices.

board_angles.q: How do you determine whether a change is within scope?
board_angles.a: I ask whether the modified work is materially different from what was competed - whether the solicitation put offerors on notice that this kind of change could occur, the magnitude relative to the original effort, and whether other firms would have competed differently; if it is outside scope it is a new procurement needing competition or a Part 6 justification.

board_angles.q: You issue a unilateral change order and the contractor disagrees with the price. What must the contractor do?
board_angles.a: Continue performance as changed - RFO FAR 43.301(b) and the Changes clause impose a duty to proceed - while asserting its right to an equitable adjustment within the period stated in the clause, normally 30 days, and we negotiate the adjustment and definitize by bilateral modification.

board_angles.q: What is the purpose of the post-award orientation, and what is inappropriate there?
board_angles.a: To align both parties on the contract as written - scope, deliverables, surveillance, invoicing, access and property, and the COR's limits stated in front of the contractor; it is inappropriate to renegotiate price or terms, to direct work beyond the contract, or to let the customer hand the contractor a to-do list.

board_angles.q: A contractor hands you an REA. Walk me through your process.
board_angles.a: Get it in writing with the clause relied on, the facts and a cost breakdown; decide entitlement before quantum; obtain the DFARS 252.243-7002 certification where required; analyze cost against the Part 31 cost principles with audit support if the dollars warrant; negotiate and definitize by bilateral modification with a release - and if it arrives as a certified claim over $100,000, I run the Contract Disputes Act clock and issue a final decision.

title: Terminations: Convenience, Default and the Commercial Path
summary: The Government holds a unique right to terminate a contract for its own convenience, and a separate right to terminate for the contractor's failure to perform. Termination for convenience buys out the contractor's incurred costs and profit on work done; termination for default is a drastic sanction that requires a documented failure, consideration of excusable causes, and usually a cure or show-cause notice first. Commercial contracts follow a shorter path under RFO FAR 12.304 with termination for cause rather than default.

sections.heading: Termination for convenience
sections.body:
Termination for convenience is exercised when it is in the Government's interest - the requirement went away, funding changed, the mission changed, or a protest corrective action requires it. It is a unilateral action taken by the contracting officer under the Termination for Convenience clause, and the contractor's remedy is a settlement rather than breach damages.

What the contractor gets:

- The contract price for completed and accepted items.
- Costs incurred on the terminated work, including a reasonable allowance for settlement expenses and subcontractor settlements.
- Profit on work actually performed. Under RFO FAR 49.202, profit is allowed on preparations made and work done, but never on the terminated - that is, unperformed - portion, and no anticipatory profit and no consequential damages are allowed. If the contract would have been a loss contract, a loss adjustment applies and profit is denied.

Process: issue the notice stating the effective date and extent; direct the contractor to stop work and preserve property; instruct on subcontract terminations; negotiate the settlement proposal. Partial terminations are common and the surviving work may need an equitable adjustment.

sections.heading: Termination for default - and what to do first
sections.body:
Termination for default is available when the contractor fails to deliver on time, fails to make progress so as to endanger performance, or fails to perform any other material provision. It is a drastic sanction. Before I sign one I consider the factors the FAR directs: the terms of the contract and the specific failure; the specific failure's effect on the Government; the availability of the supplies or services from other sources and the time to get them; the urgency of the need and the period that would be required to obtain them elsewhere; the degree of essentiality of the contractor in the Government's acquisition program and the effect on its ability to supply other contractors; the contractor's capability and whether a different approach would produce performance; the effect on the contractor's ability to liquidate progress payments; and any excusable cause.

I also coordinate with counsel, with the requiring activity on the impact, with the small business specialist if the contractor is small, and with my chain - a default that is later converted by a board or court to a termination for convenience costs the Government the settlement anyway plus the delay.

sections.heading: Cure notices and show cause notices
sections.body:
The delinquency notices are at RFO FAR 49.607 and boards ask about the ten-day rule almost every time.

- Cure notice: used when the failure is something other than a failure to deliver on time - for example, failure to make progress or failure to perform a material provision - and there is still delivery time remaining. It gives the contractor 10 days, or longer if the KO allows, to cure the condition. Before issuing it, confirm that a period at least equal to the cure period remains in the delivery schedule. If less than 10 days remain, do not issue a cure notice.
- Show cause notice: used when the time remaining is insufficient for a cure period, or when the delivery date has already passed. It tells the contractor the Government is considering termination for default and asks it to show cause why it should not be terminated, including any excusable causes, so that the KO has the facts before deciding.

Neither notice is a termination; both build the record and preserve the Government's position. Send by a method that documents receipt, and if the response establishes an excusable cause the answer is an extension, not a default.

sections.heading: Excusable delay
sections.body:
An excusable delay is a failure to perform arising from causes beyond the control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor. The Excusable Delays clause at RFO FAR 52.249-14 and the default clauses list the classic causes: acts of God or of the public enemy; acts of the Government in either its sovereign or contractual capacity; fires; floods; epidemics; quarantine restrictions; strikes; freight embargoes; and unusually severe weather.

Rules that matter:

- The delay must be beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence. A subcontractor delay is excusable only if the cause would be excusable for the prime and the items were not obtainable elsewhere in time.
- The remedy is normally a no-cost time extension, not money. Money comes only if a clause such as Government Delay of Work or Suspension of Work provides it.
- An excusable delay defeats a termination for default, which is why the show cause notice asks for it.

Handed a no-cost time extension request, say: I evaluate whether the cause is excusable under the clause, and if it is I extend the schedule by bilateral modification at no cost.

sections.heading: Commercial terminations under 12.304
sections.body:
Commercial contracts do not use Part 49 mechanics. RFO FAR 12.304 and the commercial terms clause give two routes.

- Termination for the Government's convenience: the Government pays the percentage of the contract price reflecting the percentage of work performed prior to the notice, plus reasonable charges the contractor can demonstrate from its records - and the standard is what a prudent commercial party would pay, not a Part 49 settlement proposal with cost accounting detail.
- Termination for cause: the commercial analogue to default. The Government may terminate for cause when the contractor fails to comply with contract terms or fails to provide adequate assurance of future performance. The contractor is liable to the Government for any excess reprocurement costs and the Government retains its rights for nonconforming items.

Part 49 may be used as guidance for the commercial case where it does not conflict with Part 12 and the clause. A cure or show cause notice is not required by the commercial clause, but sending one builds the record and is what a reasonable buyer would do.

sections.heading: After a default - the contractor's liabilities and the KO's next moves
sections.body:
RFO FAR 49.402-2 sets out the effect of a termination for default on a fixed-price contract.

- The Government is not liable for the contractor's costs on undelivered work and is entitled to repayment of any advance and progress payments applicable to that work.
- The Government may require the contractor to transfer title and deliver completed supplies, manufacturing materials and work in process, and pay the fair value of what it takes.
- The contractor is liable to the Government for any excess costs incurred in reprocuring supplies or services similar to those terminated - the reprocurement must be at a reasonable price and within a reasonable time, and the KO should document the reasonableness because the excess costs will be challenged.
- The Government may collect against the performance bond where one exists, and may assess liquidated damages where the clause provides for them.

Other consequences: the default is reported in CPARS and FAPIIS and follows the firm into future responsibility determinations; the contractor may appeal under the Contract Disputes Act; and an improper default converts to a convenience termination. That conversion risk is why the notice step, the excusable-cause analysis and legal review are not optional.

board_angles.q: Describe the different types of terminations available.
board_angles.a: For noncommercial contracts, termination for convenience when it is in the Government's interest with a cost-based settlement, and termination for default for failure to deliver, failure to make progress or failure to perform a material provision; for commercial contracts, RFO FAR 12.304 gives termination for the Government's convenience paying the percentage of work performed plus demonstrable charges, and termination for cause with excess reprocurement cost liability.

board_angles.q: When do you issue a cure notice versus a show cause notice?
board_angles.a: A cure notice when the failure is other than late delivery and at least 10 days of the delivery schedule remain, giving the contractor 10 days to cure; a show cause notice when insufficient time remains or the delivery date has passed, asking the contractor to show cause why it should not be terminated for default and to state any excusable causes.

board_angles.q: What factors do you consider before terminating for default?
board_angles.a: The specific failure and the contract terms, the effect on the Government, availability of the supplies or services from other sources and the time to get them, the urgency and essentiality of the requirement, the contractor's capability and whether another approach would work, the effect on progress payment liquidation, and above all whether the failure is excusable.

board_angles.q: Define an excusable delay and what the contractor gets for it.
board_angles.a: A failure to perform arising from causes beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence - acts of God, acts of the Government, fires, floods, epidemics, quarantine, strikes, embargoes, unusually severe weather - and the normal remedy is a no-cost time extension by bilateral modification, not money, unless a delay clause provides compensation.

board_angles.q: Where is profit allowed and not allowed on a fixed-price termination for convenience?
board_angles.a: Profit is allowed on preparations made and work actually performed, and it is not allowed on the terminated unperformed portion - no anticipatory profit and no consequential damages, and if the contract would have been a loss contract a loss adjustment denies profit entirely.

board_angles.q: What additional liabilities does the contractor incur after a termination for default?
board_angles.a: The Government owes nothing for undelivered work and can recover advance and progress payments applicable to it, can take title to completed supplies and work in process at fair value, and the contractor is liable for the excess costs of reprocuring similar supplies or services - plus the default record follows the firm into future responsibility determinations.
